hops.title: Stonewashed jeans may never touch a stone
hops.text: The name promises stones, but your stonewashed jeans may never have met one. The traditional method tumbled each pair in a large washing machine with a kilogram or two of pumice. An enzyme called cellulase can do the job instead. It breaks tiny fiber ends off the surface of the cotton yarn, which loosens the dye, and the rubbing of the wash carries that dye away. In this wash the substrate is cellulose, the molecule that makes up cotton fibers, and it fits cellulase's active site.

sources.citation: Kuhad RC, Gupta R, Singh A. Microbial cellulases and their industrial applications. Enzyme Research 2011:280696 (2011).

hops.title: How a Yellowstone bacterium made PCR easier
hops.text: Scientists using an early version of PCR, a method for copying DNA, had a tedious chore. Every round needed high heat, the heat ruined their copying enzyme, and they had to add fresh enzyme again and again. Relief came from a bacterium living in Yellowstone's hot springs. Its copying enzyme, Taq, survived the heat, so the chore disappeared. That heat-resistant enzyme later became a key ingredient in PCR-based tests for COVID-19. Both enzymes copied DNA, but only one could take the heat.

hops.title: Why Siamese cats have dark paws
hops.text: Why does a Siamese cat have a pale body but dark ears, paws, tail and face? In these cats, tyrosinase, the enzyme needed to make dark pigment, carries one changed building block, and the altered enzyme works better in cooler skin. About a century ago, researchers kept Siamese cats in the cold, and new fur grew in darker. Then they shaved a patch and warmed just that spot. The fur there grew back lighter. The cat's coat is a map of where cooler skin makes more pigment.
